subject: unmarkedFrameGMM and gmultmix: including dependent double-observer sampling and both primary and secondary occasions

messages.author: bb65fb84f0051bd8
messages.subject: unmarkedFrameGMM and gmultmix: including dependent double-observer sampling and both primary and secondary occasions
parts:
I am attempting to generate results from a Generalized Multinomial N-mixture Model (GMM) and following a mixture of scripts from the {unmarked} package's help files as well as this thread on the Google Group: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/FAOcx6TKF8c.

I'm interested in fitting the GMM to imaginary data, assuming a dependent double-observer approach with 2 (or more) observers (e.g., representing interannual technician turnover) in a hypothetical survey that would have 10 primary (e.g., years) and 5 secondary (e.g., replicate surveys per year, across a breeding season) periods. 

I'm also interested in adding both observer ID and Julian date as observation-level covariates in the model, but I just can't seem to get the dimensions right for occasions or observer IDs in my current tests.

Here's a snippet of my code:

########################################################################

# Example for setting up data with covariates and without fitting a model
library(unmarked)
n <- 100 #Number of sites
T <- 10 #Number of primary periods
J <- 5 #Number of secondary periods
site <- 1:100 #Site IDs
years <- data.frame(matrix(rep(2010:2019, each=n), n, T)) #Matrix of years surveyed
years <- data.frame(lapply(years, as.factor)) #Factorize the years
y <- array(rpois(n*J*T,3), c(n, 2, T)) #Matrix of counts with approximate lambda of 3 (i.e. expected local abundance per location)
occasions <- data.frame(matrix(rep(1:(J*T), each=n), n, J*T)) #Matrix of sampling occasions (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)
observers <- data.frame(matrix(rep(c("A","B"), each=n), n, J*T)) #Matrix of observer IDs (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)

#doublepiFun; see: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/FAOcx6TKF8c  
depDoubleObs <- function(p) {
  M <- nrow(p)
  pi <- matrix(NA, M, 2)
  pi[,1] <- p[,1]
  pi[,2] <- p[,2]*(1-p[,1])
  return(pi)
}
obsToY <- matrix(1, 2, 2)
numPrimary <- T
obsToY <- kronecker(diag(numPrimary), obsToY)

#Setting up the object frame
umfGMM <- unmarkedFrameGMM(y=y,
                            siteCovs = data.frame(site=site),
                            obsCovs=list(occasion=occasions, observer=observers),
                            yearlySiteCovs=data.frame(year=c(t(years))),
                            numPrimary=T, type="double", obsToY=obsToY, 
                            piFun="depDoubleObs")
##Error thrown: Error in unmarkedFrame(y, siteCovs, obsCovs, obsToY = obsToY) : 
##At least one matrix in obsCovs has incorrect number of dimensions.

########################################################################

Would anyone be willing and able to help me resolve this error? Also, would the final umfGMM be readily amenable to the Dail-Madsen frame and model (i.e. unmarkedFramePCO and pcountOpen)?

I suspect that if the dimensions of both occasions and observer IDs are corrected, then adding a new covariate like Julian date to the GMM would be relatively straightforward. I must admit that I regularly struggle with justifying object dimensionality for these kinds of tools, unfortunately.

Thanks for any help, in advance!

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: unmarkedFrameGMM and gmultmix: including dependent double-observer sampling and both primary and secondary occasions
parts:
Hi Andrew,

The dependent double observer approach with gmultmix() expects exactly two "secondary periods" within each primary period; that is, the counts from the two observers. You have to restructure a few things in the code to make that work, starting with changing J = 2:

n <- 100 #Number of sites
T <- 10 #Number of primary periods

site <- 1:100 #Site IDs
years <- data.frame(matrix(rep(2010:2019, each=n), n, T)) #Matrix of years surveyed
years <- data.frame(lapply(years, as.factor)) #Factorize the years

y <- array(rpois(n*J*T,3), c(n, J * T)) #Matrix of counts with approximate lambda of 3 (i.e. expected local abundance per location)
occasions <- data.frame(matrix(rep(1:T, each=n*J), n, J*T)) #Matrix of sampling occasions (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)
observers <- data.frame(matrix(rep(c("A","B"), each=n), n, J*T)) #Matrix of observer IDs (i.e. no. primary * secondary periods)

In this new setup the y matrix is dimensions (100, 2*T) and the column order is occasion1observer1, occasion1observer2, occasion2observer1 .... 
Also you want to provide either the type argument or obsToY/piFun arguments to unmarkedFrameGMM, but not both (in your case, the latter:

#Setting up the object frame
umfGMM <- unmarkedFrameGMM(y=y,
                            siteCovs = data.frame(site=site),
                            obsCovs=list(occasion=occasions, observer=observers),
                            yearlySiteCovs=data.frame(year=c(t(years))),

numPrimary=T, obsToY=obsToY, 
                            piFun="depDoubleObs")

With these changes I was able to construct the unmarkedFrame.

Based on your description of the hypothetical survey it also sounds like maybe what you actually want is 10 primary periods (years) each with 5 secondary periods (within years) and then within *each of those* 5 secondary periods you actually conduct the dependent double observer sampling. I don't think it is possible to fit such a model in unmarked. You can either estimate temporary emigration/availability with gmultmix() or between-year population dynamics with pcountOpen(), but not both at the same time. I could be wrong about this! One thing that probably adds to the confusion is that unmarkedFrameGMM has the "yearlySiteCovs" argument which as Richard noted should probably actually be called "primarySiteCovs" (https://github.com/rbchan/unmarked/issues/38).

Ken

messages.subject: Re: unmarkedFrameGMM and gmultmix: including dependent double-observer sampling and both primary and secondary occasions
parts:
Hi Ken,

That was very helpful. Thank you very much for the code assistance as well as for the explanation of current package capabilities. In the example above, is it true that J (the number of secondary occasions) more accurately represents the number of observers rather than the way I was interpreting?

Your suspicions about the proposed approach were correct: I actually want 10 primary periods (years) each with 5 secondary periods (within years) and then within *each of those* 5 secondary periods the dependent double observer sampling occurs.

Cheers,
Andrew
